claims.text: Hook the feet under the pad or strap at the high end of the bench and lie back with the rack slightly behind the head.

quotes.text: Secure your feet under the stirrup, bar or strap at the high end of the bench and lie flat on your back with the rack slightly behind you.

claims.text: Set the bench in decline by adjusting the backrest or raising the foot end; the EMG studies used -15 degrees (a study setting, not a technique recommendation).

quotes.text: Set a bench so that it is in decline, either by adjusting the backrest or by elevating the foot.
a free-weight barbell bench press performed at 0°, 30°, 45° and -15° bench angles
declined (-15°) bench press (DBP)

claims.text: Overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.

quotes.text: Using an overhand grip, grip the bar with your hands slightly wider than your shoulder width apart.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.

claims.text: Pull the shoulder blades together and down, chest up.

quotes.text: Lie down on the bench, pull your shoulder blades together and down, with a proud chest.

claims.text: Lower the bar with control to touch the lower chest only; do not let the bar drift (WorkoutLabs: 'too far forward'), and do not bounce it.

quotes.text: Lower the bar with control until it touches your chest.
Do not let the bar drift too far forward, it should touch down your lower chest only. Don't bounce the weight off your chest.

claims.text: A way out: set safety racks on both sides, because a failed decline rep cannot be rolled down the belly; beginners should use a spotter, or go conservative on weight without one.

quotes.text: Remember to set up safety racks on your sides while decline benching, as you cannot roll the bar down your belly if you fail.
If you are new at this exercise, you should use a spotter. If no spotter is available, then be conservative with the amount of weight used.

claims.text: Set the bar in the rack at a height you can reach without fully straightening the arms; lift it out and hold it over you on locked arms.

quotes.text: Set a barbell in a weight rack at the low end of a decline bench, making sure it is at a height you can reach without fully extending your arms.
Push up to lift the bar from the rack and hold it directly over you with your arms locked.

claims.text: Tempo used by this guide: 2 seconds down, 1-second pause, 1 second up; within ACSM's moderate 1-2 s range.

quotes.text: When performing this exercise, use a 2:1:1 count. That is a count of two on the downward movement. Pause for a count of one. A count of one one the upward movement.
using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: The lower chest works as hard on the decline as on the flat bench, and more than at 45 degrees incline.

quotes.text: The sEMG of lower pectoralis was greater during -15° (100.4 ± 5.7% MVIC), 30° (86.6 ± 4.8% MVIC) and horizontal (100.1 ± 5.2% MVIC) bench conditions compared to the 45° (71.9 ± 4.5% MVIC)
The sternocostal head was similarly excited in DBP vs. BP

claims.text: On the decline the triceps work as hard as on the flat bench; the front shoulder was measured working less than in the other presses tested, which is why it is listed as a secondary, not primary, mover.

quotes.text: Triceps brachii excitation was overall greater (d: 2.01/6.75) in BP and DBP compared to all other exercises.
Anterior deltoid was less excited (d: 3.84/19.77) in DBP compared to all other exercises.

claims.text: Add load in small steps: ACSM recommends a 2-10% increase once the current load can be done for one to two reps over the target.

quotes.text: it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number

claims.text: Barbells pressing on the neck have killed weightlifters by traumatic asphyxia; a bar that lands high on the chest, above the lower-chest touch point, is closer to the neck (inference: the sources name neck compression by barbells in general and the lower-chest touch, not this link).

quotes.text: an unrecognized source of accidental asphyxia--compression of the neck by barbells

There have been at least 11 similar deaths reported to the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) and cataloged in the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System between 1999 and 2002.
Do not let the bar drift too far forward, it should touch down your lower chest only.

claims.text: Across US emergency-department weight-training injuries, the most common mechanism was weights dropping on the person, and 90% involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

claims.text: Pec tendon ruptures happen while the loaded muscle lengthens (the lowering phase), most often on the bench press.

quotes.text: The injury results from an eccentric contracture of the muscle most commonly while performing the bench press maneuver during weight training.

claims.text: Up to 36% of documented resistance-training injuries are at the shoulder, and poor attention to technique is a named risk factor.

extrinsic risk factors, namely, that of improper attention to exercise technique

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; the decline angle, the hooked feet and the lower-chest touch point read only from the side (c1, c2, c5).
plate.equipment: Decline bench, head end low, about -15 degrees (the angle used in the EMG studies, c2), foot pads at the high end (c1), rack behind the head (c1) with safety racks at the sides (c6); barbell.
plate.start: Supine on the decline, feet hooked under the pads (c1), shoulder blades together and down (c4); bar held over the chest on locked arms (c7).
plate.end: Bar touching the lower chest (c5), feet still hooked (c1).

checkpoints.label: Feet hooked
checkpoints.what: Feet locked under the pads at the high end.

checkpoints.label: Lower-chest touch
checkpoints.what: Bar touches the lower chest only, never high toward the neck.

checkpoints.label: Blades together
checkpoints.what: Shoulder blades pulled together and down, chest up.

mistake.what: Bar landing high on the chest, toward the neck.
mistake.why: WorkoutLabs says the bar should touch the lower chest only and not drift; a high touch brings the bar toward the neck (c12, MECH). How often it happens is not measured in any source read.

grip.type: Closed overhand grip (c3); thumbs wrapped (inherited, parent c4).
grip.handContact: Bar in the base of the palm (inherited, parent c5).
grip.wrist: Straight, not bent back (inherited, parent c5).

setup.step: Set the bench in decline and set the safety racks at both sides.
Set the bar at a height you can reach without straightening your arms.
Hook your feet under the pads and lie back with the rack behind your head.
Shoulder blades together and down; grip slightly wider than your shoulders.
Lift the bar out, ideally with a spotter, and hold it over your chest on locked arms.

posture.point: Bar to the lower chest only.
Wrists straight, bar low in the palm (inherited, parent c5).

handlingMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar land high on the chest, toward the neck.
handlingMistakes.fix: Lower it to the lower chest only.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Benching heavy without safeties or a spotter.
handlingMistakes.fix: Set the safety racks; use a spotter or go lighter.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Bouncing the bar off the chest.

rows.where: Lower chest and backs of the arms
Sharp pain in the chest or front of the shoulder while lowering
Pain deep in the front of the shoulder
rows.means: Usually a warning sign; the shoulder is a common injury site in lifting.

risks.risk: Bar over the face and neck: a bar landing high on the chest moves toward the neck, and a failed rep cannot be rolled off; wrap the thumbs and set safety racks.
Adding weight in big jumps. Add 2-10% only once you can do one or two reps over your target.
Pec tendon rupture while lowering the bar.

zooms.right: Bar in the base of the palm, thumb wrapped, wrist straight.
zooms.wrong: Bar high toward the fingers, wrist bent back.

zooms.right: Both feet locked under the pads.
zooms.wrong: Feet loose, not locked under the pads.
